assessment.nobel_worthiness: Base editors fuse a deaminase to a catalytically impaired Cas protein and chemically convert one base into another at a programmed site without double-strand cleavage. This is a clear principle, a new chemical capability on the genome, and it opens enormous therapeutic and research possibilities; the discovery is easy to state to a broad audience.
assessment.attribution: Liu led the concept and the group; Komor (cytosine base editors) and Gaudelli (adenine base editors) made the two decisive molecular implementations. A Liu, Komor, Gaudelli configuration is defensible. The Kondo/Nishida deaminase-Cas9 work is parallel but I see a stronger core in the Liu lab; the Cas9/CRISPR foundation was already recognised in 2020.
assessment.maturity: Independent replication is extensive, and clinical use (including first patients treated with base editors) is emerging, so timing looks ripe. Residual issues are off-target and bystander editing and the long-term clinical record.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as chemistry rather than genome engineering after the 2020 CRISPR prize.
Whether Liu should be cited only for the broader editing programme including prime editing, which is a separate candidate.
Fair weight for the Kondo/Nishida parallel work is unresolved; I have not independently verified the priority details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterobifunctional degraders and molecular glues use small molecules to hijack E3 ligases and destroy a chosen protein, turning proximity-induced chemistry into a new therapeutic modality for targets once called undruggable. Conceptually clear, generative, and chemically original.
assessment.attribution: Crews and Deshaies conceived and first demonstrated the PROTAC concept; Handa and Ito identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, explaining glue degraders. Ciulli, Gray and others made major later contributions, so the three-person cut is difficult and I regard this attribution as contestable.
assessment.maturity: Many clinical-stage degraders and strong independent validation, with the first pivotal data now appearing. Recognition is arguably timely, though approved drugs are still few.
uncertainties: Compound discovery: PROTAC design and the thalidomide-glue mechanism may need distinct recognition.
Crowded credit with many strong claimants (Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto, Ito).
Clinical success rate is not yet established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Liquid-liquid phase separation as an organising principle for membraneless compartments imports physical-chemistry concepts (phase behaviour, multivalency, thresholds) into cell biology. As a physicist I find the quantitative framework appealing, and the idea has changed how an entire field thinks about cellular organisation.
assessment.attribution: Brangwynne and Hyman established P granules as liquid droplets; Rosen's multivalent-interaction work gave the quantitative phase-separation framework. Pappu and Mittag contributed important theory and sequence-grammar work. This is a plausible trio but credit is spread across a large community.
assessment.maturity: The concept is broadly accepted, but the physiological relevance and material state of many reported condensates are still debated, and some in vivo evidence is contested. This may be somewhat early for a clean citation.
uncertainties: Disagreement over which reported condensates reflect true phase separation in cells.
Whether the committee sees this as chemistry or biology.
Unresolved attribution among many contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Massively parallel sequencing, particularly sequencing-by-synthesis with reversible terminators and picolitre-scale parallel pyrosequencing, reduced the cost of reading genomes by orders of magnitude and enabled genomics at scale. Its impact is vast and its chemistry (reversible terminators, cluster amplification) is concrete.
assessment.attribution: Balasubramanian and Klenerman originated the chemistry underlying the Solexa/Illumina approach; Rothberg led 454 pyrosequencing. Several other contributors (Ju, Mayer) have claims, so a clear three-person cut involves judgment. I am relying on general knowledge of the history.
assessment.maturity: Technology is more than fifteen years mature and universally used; recognition is overdue rather than premature, though the field has had no single decisive moment.
uncertainties: Distribution of credit between solid-phase/cluster chemistry and emulsion/pyrosequencing approaches.
Whether the Sanger-sequencing precedent (1980) makes the committee reluctant.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Halide perovskite absorbers reached silicon-competitive efficiencies in about a decade, an exceptionally rapid rise tied to long carrier diffusion lengths and defect tolerance. Very strong energy-materials impact and an open, active physical-chemistry question about why they work so well.
assessment.attribution: Miyasaka reported the first perovskite-sensitised cell; Park and Grätzel's group and Snaith's group made the solid-state breakthroughs that triggered the field. Grätzel, Kanatzidis, and Seok also have strong claims; the allocation is hard and not obviously settled. Kojima is not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Efficiency records are confirmed repeatedly, but long-term stability, lead toxicity and commercial scale-up remain unresolved, which argues for waiting.
uncertainties: Operational stability may undercut a prize citation on practical impact.
Credit allocation among six names is unresolved.
Basic questions about the photophysics are still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reading single molecules of DNA/RNA electrically as they translocate through a nanopore is a beautiful single-molecule physics-and-chemistry idea that has become a real commercial long-read sequencer with portable, direct RNA and modification readout. It combines a clear principle, quantitative signal and new capability.
assessment.attribution: Deamer and Branton proposed and pursued the nanopore sequencing concept; Kasianowicz demonstrated polynucleotide translocation with the alpha-hemolysin pore; Bayley engineered the protein pores; Akeson showed enzyme-controlled single-nucleotide motion. The credit chain is intricate; the proposed trio follows the sequencing concept but ignores key pore-engineering work. I am uncertain about the current status of some of the credited individuals.
assessment.maturity: Independent and widely used, with long-read sequencing now routine. Timing is reasonable, but the case is split between concept, pore engineering and enzyme motor control.
uncertainties: Compound discovery with several decisive steps and no clear laureate trio.
Possible need to recognise protein-pore engineering separately.
Whether any credited individual is still living is uncertain to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: DNA origami and algorithmic DNA self-assembly show that nucleic acids can be programmed to fold into arbitrary nanoscale shapes and patterns, a bottom-up manufacturing principle with thermodynamic and kinetic design at its core. It is original and generative, and appeals to my interest in molecular machines and nanoscale devices.
assessment.attribution: Rothemund's 2006 origami is the decisive discovery; Seeman founded the field but is not in the credited names. Winfree contributed algorithmic assembly and Yan the extension to 3D and complex structures. The absence of Seeman in the supplied credit weakens any configuration I can propose.
assessment.maturity: Strong confirmation and large community, with growing applications in drug delivery and nanofabrication, but real-world impact is still emerging.
uncertainties: The founding contribution of Seeman is not among the supplied names and the field history may be hard to credit fairly.
Practical impact beyond the laboratory remains limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Noncontact AFM with a CO-functionalised tip resolves the bond skeleton of individual molecules and enabled tracking of on-surface reactions. It makes the molecular structure visible with direct, quantitative physics and is a striking approach to a fundamental limit in imaging.
assessment.attribution: Giessibl developed the qPlus force sensor and high-resolution frequency-modulation AFM; Gross, Meyer and colleagues demonstrated bond-resolved imaging with CO tips. The supplied list also includes Eigler and Ho for scanning-probe manipulation, whose contribution is more about atom control than imaging bonds, so the cut is arguable.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by multiple groups, but practical chemical impact is mostly in surface science and the technique remains specialised; this may be more a physics-leaning prize.
uncertainties: Whether the chemical significance is broad enough for the Chemistry prize.
The scanning-probe prizes of 1986 may overlap with the committee's view of the field.
